clue.text: Dig a piece of turf from the right part of Caribbean

parts.note: a dig is a cutting remark, as is a barb

indicators.note: reading from the right means the word for turf is taken backwards

parts.note: a sod is a cut piece of turf

explanation.surface: Someone cuts a square of grass from a lawn on one particular island in the West Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the right' tells you to read the turf word backwards. 'Dig' looks like a verb for cutting turf but is the noun for a jibe.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbados is an island nation forming part of the Caribbean region.

clue.text: In a flash, refrain from drinking liqueur

indicators.note: In tells us the abstaining phrase sits inside the word for a moment

parts.note: in a flash means in a moment, a mo
people who refrain from drinking are TT, teetotal: ARE TT

explanation.surface: Someone abruptly decides to stop taking alcohol, then reaches for a liqueur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals that ARE TT (are teetotal) goes inside A MO; the surface makes 'In a flash' a single phrase meaning 'suddenly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Amaretto is an almond-flavoured Italian liqueur.

clue.text: Dog needs rest after march with army officer

indicators.note: after places the word for rest behind the other two pieces

parts.note: a march is a borderland or frontier
COL is the abbreviation for colonel
to lie is to rest

explanation.surface: A dog wants a lie-down after a long march with an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'march' looks like a hike; here it is the old word for a frontier region, as in the Welsh Marches.
explanation.definitionFit: The border collie is a sheepdog breed from the Anglo-Scottish borders.

clue.text: Air or nitrogen inhaled by anybody running

indicators.note: inhaled by puts the gas symbol inside the rearranged letters
running suggests the letters of anybody are set in motion and rearranged

parts.note: N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: A question of whether anybody out jogging breathes in plain air or nitrogen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' rearranges ANYBODY to DANYBOY, and 'inhaled by' puts N inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An air is a tune, and Danny Boy is a famous Irish song set to the Londonderry Air.

clue.text: French writer pressing claim in defensive article

indicators.note: in a down clue the writer pressing on the claim sits above it

parts.note: George Sand was a French novelist
to bag something is to claim it, as in 'bags I'

explanation.surface: A French author presses a claim in an article written in defence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bag' as claim is the playground 'bags I first go'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandbag is used in fortifications and flood barriers, so it is an article of defence.

clue.text: Drink for one lifting medal

parts.note: for one means for example, abbreviated eg

indicators.note: lifting in a down clue says the medal word reads upwards

parts.note: gong is slang for a medal

explanation.surface: A drink for someone raising a medal in triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifting' turns GONG into GNOG beneath EG.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is a drink of eggs, milk and often spirits.

clue.text: US rallying champion more foolhardy when cutting corners

indicators.note: cutting the corners takes off the first and last letters

parts.note: rasher is the comparative of rash, foolhardy

explanation.surface: An American rally driver who takes more risks by cutting corners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rallying' suggests motor sport, but the champion is Arthur Ashe, the tennis player, rallies being exchanges of shots.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe was an American tennis champion, and tennis players rally.

clue.text: Halt in city construction emptied plant

indicators.note: in places the word for halt inside the remaining letters
emptied means the insides of both words are removed, leaving the outer letters

parts.note: halt is an old word for lame

explanation.surface: A stoppage on a city building site has left the plant deserted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'emptied' strips both words to their outer letters, and the halt word sits inside the second pair. 'Halt' reads as a stop but means limping.
explanation.definitionFit: The cyclamen is a flowering plant with upswept petals.

clue.text: Some Welsh ground, I agree, turns with spin

parts.note: an angle is a slant or spin put on a story

indicators.note: turns says the word of agreement is read backwards

parts.note: yes expresses agreement

explanation.surface: Someone agrees that a patch of Welsh land rotates as it spins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses the word of agreement, which follows the spin word; 'with' is a link. 'spin' looks like part of the turning picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglesey is an island off north-west Wales, so a piece of Welsh territory.

clue.text: Earth, very fine, held in both hands

indicators.note: held in says the excellent term goes between the two hands

parts.note: L and R, left and right hands
A1 means first-rate, written AI

explanation.surface: Fine soil is cupped carefully in both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earth' is a fox's den, not soil.
explanation.definitionFit: An earth is a burrowing animal's den, the same as a lair.

clue.text: Tailless dog, Lear character and beauty told of in nursery rhyme

indicators.note: tailless says the last letter of the dog is cut off

parts.note: a dingo is an Australian wild dog
the Dong with a Luminous Nose is a creature in Edward Lear's nonsense verse

indicators.note: told of says the word for a beauty is heard, not seen

parts.note: a belle is a beauty

explanation.surface: A list of characters from children's stories and nonsense verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lear' tempts towards King Lear; it is Edward Lear the nonsense poet. BELLE said out loud gives BELL.
explanation.definitionFit: Ding Dong Bell is a traditional nursery rhyme about a cat in a well.

clue.text: One screwed up career in squash

indicators.note: in places the word for rushing inside the squash

parts.note: butternut is a kind of squash
to career is to rush, to fly

explanation.surface: Someone's career has been ruined while playing squash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'career' looks like a job but is the verb for rushing headlong; 'squash' is the vegetable, not the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A butterfly nut is a wing nut, tightened by screwing it up by hand.

clue.text: Repair to bar after receiving hard beating

indicators.note: after receiving says the rearranged letters take in the abbreviation
re-pair suggests the letters are paired up again in a new order

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone retires to the pub after taking a hard beating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repair' reads as 'go' but rearranges TO BAR into ATROB, which takes in H after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Athrob means pulsing or throbbing, as a heart beats.

clue.text: Unease with last of capital going virtually no distance!

parts.note: angst is anxiety or unease

indicators.note: last of points at the final letter of the capital
going says that final letter departs

parts.note: Rome is the Italian capital

explanation.surface: Anxiety as the capital's last resident moves almost no distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last of capital going' leaves ROM from ROME; 'with' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: An angstrom is a unit of length of one ten-billionth of a metre, a tiny distance.

clue.text: Place handle from lead on setter's back

parts.note: to be on top is to lead

indicators.note: back says the possessive word is reversed

parts.note: the setter's means my, from the setter's own view

explanation.surface: A handle placed on a dog's lead at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns MY into YM; 'handle' is slang for a name.
explanation.definitionFit: A toponym is a place name, and handle is slang for a name.

clue.text: League champions do places for VIPs

definitions.meaning: winners of a league finish at the head of the standings
the table for honoured guests at a banquet or wedding

explanation.surface: Football winners get the seats reserved for important guests.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is the verb phrase: league champions top the table.
explanation.definitionFit: At a formal dinner the head table seats the most important guests.

clue.text: With this singer dressed for choir?

parts.note: choristers are dressed in robes
the singer's name, split, describes being dressed with robes on

explanation.surface: A singer kitted out to join a church choir.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the trick: split the singer's name in two and it describes wearing choir vestments.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Robeson was an American bass singer and actor.

clue.text: Old Irish politician turned up in Enniskillen? No, Cork

indicators.note: turned up says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A historic Irish politician appears not in Enniskillen but in Cork.
explanation.walkthrough: Daniel O'Connell, the Liberator, campaigned for Catholic emancipation; the name hides upwards across 'Enniskillen? No, Cork'.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel O'Connell was a nineteenth-century Irish political leader.

clue.text: Authoritative viewer's in possession of right answer

indicators.note: in possession of says the eye word holds the two abbreviations

parts.note: ocular means of the eye, the viewer's organ
R for right and A for answer

explanation.surface: An expert's eye holds the correct response.
explanation.walkthrough: 'viewer's' reads as a person's possessive but stands for the adjective of the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Oracular pronouncements come with the authority of an oracle.

clue.text: West Virginian's cut bud on minute tree

parts.note: an American, such as a Virginian, cuts with an ax, the US spelling of axe
bud is American slang for a pal

explanation.surface: A West Virginian prunes a bud on a tiny tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West Virginian' looks like one phrase but splits: W, then the Virginian's (American) spelling AX.
explanation.definitionFit: The wax palm is a tall South American palm tree that yields wax.

clue.text: Girl quietly hid, all worried about nudity ultimately

parts.note: P, piano, means quietly in music

indicators.note: about says the rearranged letters surround the final letter
worried suggests the letters of hid all are agitated into a new order
ultimately picks the last letter of nudity

explanation.surface: A girl hid quietly, anxious about being seen naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' rearranges the hid-all letters to HLLIDA, and 'about' wraps that round the last letter of nudity; 'quietly' is the musical P in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Phyllida is a female first name, so a girl.

clue.text: Eskimo conserving heat at last makes sense

indicators.note: conserving says the people's name keeps the letter within it

parts.note: the Inuit are an Eskimo people

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of heat

explanation.surface: Arctic people keep warm in a way that is sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: T goes inside INUIT after the N; 'makes' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To intuit is to sense or perceive something without reasoning.

clue.text: Recalled perfectly fine female in love with postman

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, O
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
Postman Pat is the title character of a British children's TV series

explanation.surface: A fine woman falls for the postman.
explanation.walkthrough: Postman Pat is a British children's television postman.
explanation.definitionFit: Something known off pat is memorised and recalled perfectly.

clue.text: Fortune obtained from a woman touring fair

indicators.note: touring says the woman's name goes round the word for fair

parts.note: Penny is a woman's name
fair means pretty

explanation.surface: A woman makes a fortune touring the fairground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring' wraps a woman with a leading A round the word for fair; 'obtained from' is a link joining definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretty penny is an idiom for a large sum of money.

clue.text: One's iced beer, perhaps, has no head

indicators.note: has no head removes the first letter, with a nod to beer's froth

parts.note: beer is an example of a drink

explanation.surface: A chilled beer is served without its frothy head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' plays on a beer's froth; it takes the D off DRINK.
explanation.definitionFit: A skating rink is a surface that is frozen over, something iced.

clue.text: Invalid in duel, old, ignoring odds

indicators.note: ignoring odds means taking only the even-placed letters of the run

explanation.surface: An old duel was declared invalid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invalid' looks like a sick person but is the adjective meaning void.
explanation.definitionFit: Null means void or having no legal force, as in null and void.

clue.text: Some Liberals holding with fascism initially? I refuse to go there!

indicators.note: holding says the Ls surround the other pieces

parts.note: several Liberals gives several Ls, L being the abbreviation for Liberal
and means with

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of fascism

explanation.surface: A Liberal, asked to visit a fascist gathering, declares 'I refuse to go there!'
explanation.walkthrough: The first L holds AND F I in front of the other two Ls; 'refuse' is the noun for rubbish, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A landfill site is where rubbish is dumped.

clue.text: Nursery gardener questioned fences I put down in the field

indicators.note: fences means encloses, so the name surrounds the other pieces

parts.note: Mary, Mary, quite contrary is asked in the nursery rhyme how her garden grows
lit means landed, put down

explanation.surface: A nursery gardener asks questions about fences being put up in the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put down' is the past of alight, LIT; 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary' is a nursery rhyme asking how her garden grows.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the field means on active service, a military matter.
